nodes.label: Internal law of composition / Loi de composition interne
nodes.statement: A binary operation on a set $E$ is a function $\mu\colon E\times E\to E$. We write $xy$ or $x*y$ for $\mu(x,y)$. Being defined for every pair and having values in $E$ is part of this definition. An external law has a possibly different set of operators; group actions below are one example.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §1, no. 1, Definition 1; §3, no. 1 for external laws.

bibliography.locator: I, §1, no. 1, Definition 1; §3, no. 1 for external laws.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [ST-D09](../cartography.md#st-d09), [ST-D11](../cartography.md#st-d11).
uses [ST-D09](../cartography.md#st-d09), [ST-D11](../cartography.md#st-d11).

nodes.label: Magma
nodes.statement: A magma is a set $E$ equipped with one internal law of composition. The operation is part of the data: $(\mathbb Z,+)$ and $(\mathbb Z,\cdot)$ are different magmas on the same set.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D01](#as-d01), [ST-D42](../cartography.md#st-d42)

nodes.label: Associativity / Associativité
nodes.statement: An operation on $E$ is associative when $(xy)z=x(yz)$ for all $x,y,z\in E$.

nodes.label: Commutativity / Commutativité
nodes.statement: An operation on $E$ is commutative when $xy=yx$ for all $x,y\in E$. Without this global condition, a particular pair $x,y$ is said to commute when that equality holds.

nodes.label: Identity axiom / Existence d'un élément neutre
nodes.statement: There exists $e\in E$ with $ex=xe=x$ for all $x\in E$. A left identity satisfies only the first equality and a right identity only the second. An identity in this chapter is two-sided.

nodes.label: Inverse axiom / Existence des inverses
nodes.statement: For a monoid $(M,\cdot,e)$, every $x\in M$ has some $y\in M$ with $xy=yx=e$. Associativity and identity belong to the monoid hypothesis; this axiom adds invertibility of every element.

nodes.label: Left distributivity / Distributivité à gauche
nodes.statement: For two operations $+$ and $\cdot$ on $E$, left distributivity of multiplication over addition means $x(y+z)=xy+xz$ for all $x,y,z\in E$.

nodes.label: Right distributivity / Distributivité à droite
nodes.statement: Right distributivity means $(x+y)z=xz+yz$ for all $x,y,z\in E$. Both distributive laws are required for a ring, whose multiplication need not commute.

nodes.label: Nontriviality / Condition $0\ne1$
nodes.statement: For a ring, impose $0\ne1$. This is a defining condition for domains and division rings. It is not imposed on every ring.

nodes.label: Associative magma / Magma associatif; semigroup
nodes.statement: An associative magma is a magma satisfying associativity. We use semigroup as a synonym, with the empty-carrier convention stated in §1.2. No identity is required.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §1, no. 3, under the name associative magma.

bibliography.locator: I, §1, no. 3, under the name associative magma.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-A01](#as-a01)
uses [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-A01](#as-a01)

nodes.label: Commutative magma / Magma commutatif
nodes.statement: A commutative magma satisfies $xy=yx$. It need not be associative. The adjectives associative and commutative express separate conditions.

direct_dependencies.note: Immediate parent structure explicitly used in this definition.
uses [AS-A02](#as-a02)

nodes.label: Unital magma / Magma unifère
nodes.statement: A unital magma is a magma with an identity element. Its identity is unique, so it can be included in the notation $(E,\cdot,e)$ without making a choice between several candidates.

direct_dependencies.note: Immediate parent structure explicitly used in this definition.
uses [AS-A03](#as-a03)

nodes.label: Monoid / Monoïde
nodes.statement: A monoid is an associative unital magma. A commutative monoid additionally satisfies commutativity. Both $(\mathbb N,+,0)$ and $(\mathbb N,\cdot,1)$ are commutative monoids.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D03](#as-d03), [AS-D05](#as-d05)
uses [AS-D03](#as-d03), [AS-D05](#as-d05)

nodes.label: Invertible element / Élément inversible
nodes.statement: In a monoid $M$, an element $x$ is invertible if some $y$ satisfies $xy=yx=e$. Its unique inverse is denoted $x^{-1}$. The invertible elements form the set $M^\times$. A left inverse only satisfies $yx=e$; a right inverse only satisfies $xy=e$.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D06](#as-d06)

nodes.label: Cancellable element / Élément simplifiable
nodes.statement: In a magma, $a$ is left cancellable when $ax=ay$ implies $x=y$, and right cancellable when $xa=ya$ implies $x=y$. A cancellative magma has both properties for every element. Cancellation alone does not assert the existence of an identity or inverses.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D02](#as-d02)

nodes.label: Homomorphism and isomorphism of magmas and monoids
nodes.statement: A magma homomorphism $f\colon E\to F$ satisfies $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$. A monoid homomorphism also satisfies $f(e_E)=e_F$. An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism of the indicated type; its inverse is then a homomorphism. An endomorphism has the same source and target, and an automorphism is an isomorphism from a structure to itself. Preservation of the identity is not automatic for an arbitrary magma homomorphism between monoids.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [ST-D11](../cartography.md#st-d11), [ST-D12](../cartography.md#st-d12), [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06)
uses [ST-D11](../cartography.md#st-d11), [ST-D12](../cartography.md#st-d12), [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06)
uses [ST-D11](../cartography.md#st-d11), [ST-D12](../cartography.md#st-d12), [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06)
uses [ST-D11](../cartography.md#st-d11), [ST-D12](../cartography.md#st-d12), [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06)

nodes.label: Stable subset, submagma and generated substructure
nodes.statement: A subset $A\subseteq E$ is stable under multiplication if $xy\in A$ whenever $x,y\in A$. With the restricted operation it is a submagma. A submonoid of $M$ is a stable subset containing $e_M$. The submagma or submonoid generated by $X$ is the smallest such substructure containing $X$, equivalently the intersection of all such substructures. The distinction matters for $X=\varnothing$: the generated submagma is empty, whereas the generated submonoid is $\{e\}$.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06), [ST-D05](../cartography.md#st-d05)
uses [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06), [ST-D05](../cartography.md#st-d05)
uses [AS-D02](#as-d02), [AS-D06](#as-d06), [ST-D05](../cartography.md#st-d05)

nodes.label: Congruence / Relation d'équivalence compatible
nodes.statement: A congruence on a magma is an equivalence relation $\sim$ such that $x\sim x'$ and $y\sim y'$ imply $xy\sim x'y'$. For a ring it must be compatible with both addition and multiplication. The word congruence here refers to this general compatibility property.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [ST-D15](../cartography.md#st-d15), [AS-D01](#as-d01).
uses [ST-D15](../cartography.md#st-d15), [AS-D01](#as-d01).

nodes.label: Quotient magma or monoid / Magma ou monoïde quotient
nodes.statement: For a congruence on $E$, define $[x][y]=[xy]$ on $E/{\sim}$. If $E$ is a monoid, the class $[e]$ is the quotient identity. Write $q(x)=[x]$ for the canonical projection.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D11](#as-d11), [ST-D15](../cartography.md#st-d15)
uses [AS-D11](#as-d11), [ST-D15](../cartography.md#st-d15)

nodes.label: Direct product / Produit direct
nodes.statement: For a family $(E_i)_{i\in I}$ of magmas, equip $\prod_iE_i$ with coordinatewise multiplication. For monoids use the identity tuple $(e_i)$. The empty product is the one-element structure. The same coordinatewise construction applies to groups and, with two operations, to rings.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [ST-D18](../cartography.md#st-d18), [AS-D01](#as-d01)
uses [ST-D18](../cartography.md#st-d18), [AS-D01](#as-d01)

nodes.label: Opposite law / Loi opposée
nodes.statement: The opposite magma $E^{\mathrm{op}}$ has the same set and product $x\star y=yx$. For a ring, only multiplication is reversed; addition is unchanged. Associativity, identity and the group property pass to the opposite. Reversing twice recovers the original law.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D01](#as-d01), [AS-D02](#as-d02).

nodes.label: Uniqueness of the identity
nodes.statement: A magma has at most one two-sided identity. More generally, if $l$ is a left identity and $r$ a right identity, then $l=r$, and this common element is a two-sided identity.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-A03](#as-a03)
proved-using [AS-D01](#as-d01).

nodes.label: Associativity and order of finite products
nodes.statement: In an associative magma, every parenthesisation of the same nonempty ordered list gives the same product. If the elements commute pairwise, permuting their order also leaves the product unchanged. In a monoid, the empty product is its identity. Thus associativity removes brackets; reordering requires the additional commuting hypothesis.

direct_dependencies.note: proved-using [NS-T03](number_systems.md#ns-t03).

nodes.label: Uniqueness and multiplication of inverses
nodes.statement: In a monoid, if $yx=e$ and $xz=e$, then $y=z$. Hence a two-sided inverse is unique. If $x,y$ are invertible, then $(xy)^{-1}=y^{-1}x^{-1}$, $(x^{-1})^{-1}=x$, and $e^{-1}=e$. A one-sided inverse by itself need not be two-sided.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D07](#as-d07)
proved-using [AS-A01](#as-a01), [AS-A03](#as-a03).
proved-using [AS-A01](#as-a01), [AS-A03](#as-a03).

nodes.label: Group of units / Groupe des éléments inversibles
nodes.statement: For a monoid $M$, the set $M^\times$ is a group under the restricted multiplication, with the same identity. A monoid homomorphism maps units to units and preserves their inverses. For commutative $M$, this group is abelian.

direct_dependencies.note: proved-using [AS-T03](#as-t03).

nodes.label: Invertibility implies cancellation; finite cancellation implies a group
nodes.statement: An invertible element of a monoid is cancellable on both sides. Every finite cancellative monoid is a group: multiplication by an element is an injective self-map of a finite set and hence is surjective, supplying inverses. Finiteness is essential; $(\mathbb N,+,0)$ is cancellative but is not a group.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §2, nos. 2–3, for cancellation and inverses; the finite-monoid consequence follows by the indicated argument.

bibliography.locator: I, §2, nos. 2–3, for cancellation and inverses; the finite-monoid consequence follows by the indicated argument.

nodes.label: Composition and inversion of homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Identity maps and composites are homomorphisms. The inverse of a bijective magma homomorphism is a magma homomorphism. The same assertion holds for monoid homomorphisms, with identities preserved. Therefore isomorphism is an equivalence relation on structures of a fixed type.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D09](#as-d09)
proved-using [ST-D13](../cartography.md#st-d13).

nodes.label: Intersections, images and generated substructures
nodes.statement: Intersections of submagmas of a fixed magma are submagmas, and intersections of submonoids of a fixed monoid are submonoids; the empty intersection is the whole ambient structure. Images and inverse images under homomorphisms are substructures of the indicated type. For a homomorphism $f$, the image of the substructure generated by $X$ is the substructure generated by $f(X)$. Generated substructures therefore exist and are unique.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D09](#as-d09), [AS-D10](#as-d10)
uses [AS-D09](#as-d09), [AS-D10](#as-d10)
proved-using [ST-D05](../cartography.md#st-d05), [ST-T06](../cartography.md#st-t06).
proved-using [ST-D05](../cartography.md#st-d05), [ST-T06](../cartography.md#st-t06).

nodes.label: Quotient operation and its factorisation property
nodes.statement: A congruence makes the quotient operation well-defined. The projection $q\colon E\to E/{\sim}$ is a surjective homomorphism. Any homomorphism $f\colon E\to F$ constant on equivalence classes factors uniquely as $f=\bar f\circ q$, where $\bar f$ is a homomorphism. Associativity, commutativity and an identity pass to the quotient when present. For monoid maps the factor map also preserves the identity.

direct_dependencies.note: proved-using [ST-T08](../cartography.md#st-t08).

nodes.label: Products and their universal property
nodes.statement: Coordinatewise operations make products of magmas, monoids, groups or rings into structures of the same type. Given homomorphisms $f_i\colon X\to E_i$, there is a unique homomorphism $f\colon X\to\prod_iE_i$ with $\pi_i\circ f=f_i$. Products of domains or fields need not be domains or fields: two nonzero factors give nonzero elements $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ whose product is zero. For arbitrary magmas, the underlying product may be empty; no choice principle asserting nonemptiness is used.

direct_dependencies.note: proved-using [ST-T40](../cartography.md#st-t40).

nodes.label: Group / Groupe
nodes.statement: A group is a monoid in which every element is invertible. Its data may be written $(G,\cdot,e)$, since inverses are uniquely determined. The one-element group is allowed. The additive integers $(\mathbb Z,+,0)$ are a group.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D06](#as-d06), [AS-A04](#as-a04)
uses [AS-D06](#as-d06), [AS-A04](#as-a04)

nodes.label: Abelian group / Groupe commutatif ou abélien
nodes.statement: An abelian group is a group with commutative multiplication. Additive notation is often used: the identity is $0$ and the inverse of $x$ is $-x$. Addition on $\mathbb Z,\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ gives examples.

direct_dependencies.note: Immediate parent structure explicitly used in this definition.
uses [AS-A02](#as-a02)

nodes.label: Subgroup / Sous-groupe
nodes.statement: A subset $H\subseteq G$ is a subgroup if it contains $e$ and is closed under multiplication and inverses. Its operations are the restrictions of those of $G$. Write $H\le G$; here the symbol denotes the subgroup relation, not an order on elements of $G$.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §4, no. 3, specialised to ordinary groups.

bibliography.locator: I, §4, no. 3, specialised to ordinary groups.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D15](#as-d15), [AS-D10](#as-d10)
uses [AS-D15](#as-d15), [AS-D10](#as-d10)

nodes.label: Generated subgroup / Sous-groupe engendré
nodes.statement: For $X\subseteq G$, the subgroup $\langle X\rangle$ is the intersection of the subgroups containing $X$. Its elements are finite products of elements of $X$ and their inverses, including the empty product $e$. In particular $\langle\varnothing\rangle=\{e\}$.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D17](#as-d17), [AS-T02](#as-t02)
uses [AS-D17](#as-d17), [AS-T02](#as-t02)

nodes.label: Powers, order of an element and monogenous groups
nodes.statement: For $g\in G$, define $g^0=e$, $g^{n+1}=g^ng$ and $g^{-n}=(g^{-1})^n$. The order of $g$ is the least positive integer $n$ with $g^n=e$, if such an integer exists; otherwise it is infinite. A group generated by one element is monogenous (*monogène*). Following Bourbaki's distinction, a finite monogenous group is cyclic (*cyclique*); “infinite cyclic” is a common modern synonym for infinite monogenous.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D18](#as-d18), [AS-D07](#as-d07), [NS-T02](number_systems.md#ns-t02), [NS-T06](number_systems.md#ns-t06)

nodes.label: Group homomorphism, kernel and image
nodes.statement: A group homomorphism $f\colon G\to H$ preserves multiplication. It automatically preserves identities and inverses. Its kernel is $\ker f=\{g:f(g)=e_H\}$ and its image is $f[G]$. Group isomorphisms are bijective group homomorphisms.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D15](#as-d15), [ST-D14](../cartography.md#st-d14)
uses [AS-D15](#as-d15), [ST-D14](../cartography.md#st-d14)

nodes.label: Cosets and index / Classes et indice
nodes.statement: For $H\le G$, a left coset is $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$ and a right coset is $Hg=\{hg:h\in H\}$. The index $[G:H]$ is the cardinality of the set of left cosets. Write $G/H$ for the left-coset set even when it does not carry a quotient-group operation.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §5, nos. 4–5, applied to cosets and homogeneous sets.

bibliography.locator: I, §5, nos. 4–5, applied to cosets and homogeneous sets.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D17](#as-d17), [ST-D36](../cartography.md#st-d36)
uses [AS-D17](#as-d17), [ST-D36](../cartography.md#st-d36)

nodes.label: Normal subgroup / Sous-groupe distingué
nodes.statement: A subgroup $N$ of $G$ is normal, written $N\trianglelefteq G$, when $gNg^{-1}=N$ for every $g\in G$. Equivalently, $gN=Ng$ for every $g$. Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.

nodes.label: Quotient group / Groupe quotient
nodes.statement: For $N\trianglelefteq G$, define $(gN)(hN)=(gh)N$ on $G/N$. Its identity is $N$ and $(gN)^{-1}=g^{-1}N$. The projection is $q(g)=gN$. Normality is the hypothesis ensuring that the displayed multiplication does not depend on representatives.

direct_dependencies.note: uses [AS-D21](#as-d21), [AS-D22](#as-d22)
uses [AS-D21](#as-d21), [AS-D22](#as-d22)

nodes.label: Centre and centraliser / Centre et centralisateur
nodes.statement: For $X\subseteq G$, its centraliser is $C_G(X)=\{g:gx=xg\text{ for all }x\in X\}$. The centre is $Z(G)=C_G(G)$. Both are subgroups, and the centre is a normal abelian subgroup. The notation $Z(G)$ is unrelated to the integer set $\mathbb Z$.

direct_dependencies.note: proved-using [AS-T03](#as-t03) for the asserted subgroup properties.

nodes.label: Equations and cancellation in a group
nodes.statement: For $a,b\in G$, the equation $ax=b$ has the unique solution $x=a^{-1}b$, and $ya=b$ has the unique solution $y=ba^{-1}$. In particular both cancellation laws hold. For integers $m,n$, $g^{m+n}=g^mg^n$ and $(g^m)^n=g^{mn}$; the identity $(gh)^n=g^nh^n$ holds when $g$ and $h$ commute, but is not a general group law.

nodes.label: Subgroup criterion and generated subgroups
nodes.statement: A nonempty subset $H\subseteq G$ is a subgroup exactly when $xy^{-1}\in H$ for all $x,y\in H$. Intersections of subgroups are subgroups, with empty intersection $G$. The intersection definition of $\langle X\rangle$ agrees with the finite-word description. Images and inverse images of subgroups under group homomorphisms are subgroups.

nodes.label: Identities, inverses and kernels under group maps
nodes.statement: A multiplication-preserving map between groups satisfies $f(e)=e$ and $f(g^{-1})=f(g)^{-1}$. Its kernel is normal, its image is a subgroup, and it is injective exactly when its kernel is $\{e\}$. These assertions follow directly from group arithmetic, without assuming the isomorphism theorem.

nodes.label: Coset partition and Lagrange's theorem
nodes.statement: Left cosets of $H\le G$ partition $G$, and $h\mapsto gh$ is a bijection $H\to gH$. For finite $G$, $|G|=[G:H]|H|$. Consequently the order of any element divides $|G|$. The finite statement uses no choice of representatives for an infinite quotient.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §5, nos. 4–5, counting orbits and cosets.

nodes.label: Normality and well-defined quotient multiplication
nodes.statement: For a subgroup $N\le G$, the formula $(gN)(hN)=ghN$ is well-defined on left cosets exactly when $N$ is normal. In that case it gives a group, and the projection is a surjective homomorphism with kernel $N$. A group homomorphism $f\colon G\to H$ factors uniquely through this projection exactly when $N\subseteq\ker f$.

nodes.label: First isomorphism theorem for groups
nodes.statement: For a group homomorphism $f\colon G\to H$, the map $g\ker f\mapsto f(g)$ is an isomorphism $G/\ker f\cong f[G]$. The image need not be all of $H$.

nodes.label: Correspondence and iterated quotients of groups
nodes.statement: For $N\trianglelefteq G$, inverse image under $G\to G/N$ gives an inclusion-preserving bijection between subgroups of $G/N$ and subgroups of $G$ containing $N$; normal subgroups correspond. If $N\subseteq H$ and both are normal in $G$, then $(G/N)/(H/N)\cong G/H$. If $H\le G$ and $N\trianglelefteq G$, then $HN$ is a subgroup and $H/(H\cap N)\cong HN/N$.

direct_dependencies.note: proved-using [AS-T14](#as-t14), [AS-T15](#as-t15).
proved-using [AS-T14](#as-t14), [AS-T15](#as-t15).

nodes.label: Classification of monogenous groups
nodes.statement: Every subgroup of $(\mathbb Z,+)$ is $n\mathbb Z$ for a unique $n\ge0$. The map $k\mapsto g^k$ maps $\mathbb Z$ onto $\langle g\rangle$. Hence a monogenous group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$ or to $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ for a unique $n\ge1$. Every subgroup of a monogenous group is monogenous. For $g$ of finite order $n$, $g^k=e$ exactly when $n\mid k$.

nodes.label: Monoid and group action / Monoïde ou groupe opérant sur un ensemble
nodes.statement: A left action of a monoid $M$ on a set $X$ is a function $M\times X\to X$, written $(m,x)\mapsto m\cdot x$, with $e\cdot x=x$ and $(mn)\cdot x=m\cdot(n\cdot x)$. For a group the same definition applies. A group action is faithful if the only element fixing every point is $e$, and transitive if $X$ is nonempty and any point can be moved to any other point.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §5, nos. 1 and 5. This specialises the external laws of I, §3.

nodes.label: Orbit and stabiliser / Orbite et stabilisateur
nodes.statement: For a group acting on $X$, the orbit of $x$ is $G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$ and the stabiliser is $G_x=\{g:g\cdot x=x\}$. The orbit set is denoted $X/G$. The stabiliser of a point is a subgroup; it need not be normal.

nodes.label: Permutation representation and Cayley's theorem
nodes.statement: The bijections $X\to X$ form a group $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ under composition. Giving a group action on $X$ is equivalent to giving a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Sym}(X)$. Its kernel consists of the elements fixing every point. The action of $G$ on itself by left multiplication is faithful, so every group is isomorphic to a subgroup of a permutation group.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §5, no. 1, actions and the regular permutation representation.

nodes.label: Orbit partition and orbit–stabiliser theorem
nodes.statement: Orbits partition $X$. For each $x\in X$, $G_x$ is a subgroup and $gG_x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is a bijection $G/G_x\to G\cdot x$. For finite $G$, $|G\cdot x|=[G:G_x]$ and $|G|=|G_x|\,|G\cdot x|$.

nodes.label: Words and free monoid / Mots et monoïde libre
nodes.statement: For a set $X$, let $X^*=\coprod_{n\in\mathbb N}X^n$ be its finite words, with length included in the disjoint-union encoding. Multiplication is concatenation and the identity is the empty word. Identify $X$ with the words of length one. In this entry the star denotes words; it does not mean the units $M^\times$ of a monoid.

nodes.label: Universal property of the free monoid
nodes.statement: Concatenation makes $X^*$ a monoid. Every function $f\colon X\to M$ to a monoid extends uniquely to a monoid homomorphism $\widehat f\colon X^*\to M$, sending a word $x_1\cdots x_n$ to $f(x_1)\cdots f(x_n)$ and the empty word to $e_M$. Thus $\mathbb N$ under addition is the free monoid on one generator, by word length.

nodes.label: Ring / Anneau
nodes.statement: A ring $(R,+,\cdot,0,1)$ has an abelian additive group $(R,+,0)$, a multiplicative monoid $(R,\cdot,1)$, and both distributive laws. Multiplication need not commute. The zero ring has one element and $0=1$. The conditions on addition, multiplication and distributivity correspond to Bourbaki's three ring-axiom groups AN I–III.

nodes.label: Commutative ring / Anneau commutatif
nodes.statement: A commutative ring is a ring whose multiplication is commutative. Addition is already commutative in every ring. The integers with their usual two operations form a commutative ring.

direct_dependencies.note: Immediate parent structure explicitly used in this definition.

nodes.label: Ring homomorphism, kernel and image
nodes.statement: A ring homomorphism $f\colon R\to S$ satisfies $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$, $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$ and $f(1_R)=1_S$. It then preserves zero and additive opposites. Set $\ker f=\{r:f(r)=0_S\}$. A ring isomorphism is a bijective ring homomorphism. We do not use “homomorphism” here for maps that fail to preserve $1$.

nodes.label: Subring and generated subring / Sous-anneau
nodes.statement: A subring $S\subseteq R$ contains $1_R$ and is closed under addition, additive opposites and multiplication. Its zero and one agree with those of $R$. The subring generated by $X\subseteq R$ is the intersection of all subrings containing $X$. It contains the image of the integers even when $X$ is empty.

nodes.label: Left, right and two-sided ideal / Idéal
nodes.statement: A left ideal $I$ is an additive subgroup of $R$ with $RI\subseteq I$; a right ideal satisfies $IR\subseteq I$. A two-sided ideal satisfies both. In a commutative ring these notions agree and we simply say ideal. An ideal is proper if $I\ne R$. The ideal generated by a subset is the smallest ideal of the specified kind containing it. In a commutative ring, the principal ideal $(a)$ is $Ra$.

nodes.label: Quotient ring / Anneau quotient
nodes.statement: For a two-sided ideal $I$, the additive cosets $R/I$ carry operations $(a+I)+(b+I)=(a+b)+I$ and $(a+I)(b+I)=ab+I$. Their zero and one are $I$ and $1+I$. The projection is $q(a)=a+I$. A quotient ring is allowed to be zero, as happens for $I=R$.

nodes.label: Ring units, zero divisors and nilpotent elements
nodes.statement: The units of $R$ are the invertible elements of its multiplicative monoid, denoted $R^\times$. A nonzero element $a$ is a zero divisor if $ab=0$ or $ba=0$ for some nonzero $b$; when necessary we state the side explicitly. An element is nilpotent if $a^n=0$ for some positive integer $n$. In a nonzero ring, zero is not a unit. These are properties of multiplication, distinct from additive invertibility, which every element has.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §8, nos. 1–2, for units, zero products and nilpotence.

bibliography.locator: I, §8, nos. 1–2, for units, zero products and nilpotence.

nodes.label: Elementary ring identities and the zero ring
nodes.statement: For all $a,b\in R$, $a0=0a=0$, $(-a)b=a(-b)=-(ab)$ and $(-a)(-b)=ab$. A ring has $0=1$ exactly when it has one element. Its units form a group. In a nonzero ring no unit is a zero divisor, and every nonzero nilpotent element is a zero divisor. Cancellation of a factor in a product requires an appropriate cancellability hypothesis.

nodes.label: Ideals, generators and the identity
nodes.statement: Intersections of left, right or two-sided ideals are ideals of the same kind, so generated ideals exist. The two-sided ideal generated by $X$ consists of finite sums $\sum_i r_ix_is_i$ with $x_i\in X$ and $r_i,s_i\in R$, including the empty sum. A left or right ideal containing $1$ is all of $R$. Consequently a proper ideal cannot be a subring under our common-identity convention.

nodes.label: Ring maps, subrings and kernels
nodes.statement: A ring homomorphism preserves $0$, additive opposites, units and inverses of units. Its image is a subring; its kernel is a two-sided ideal. It is injective exactly when its kernel is zero. Images and inverse images of subrings are subrings. Inverse images of ideals are ideals of the same side; images of ideals are ideals in the image ring, and hence in the target ring when the map is surjective. Intersections of subrings are subrings, so generated subrings exist.

nodes.label: Quotient rings and the first isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: For a two-sided ideal $I$, the quotient operations are well-defined and make $R/I$ a ring. A ring homomorphism $f\colon R\to S$ factors uniquely through $R/I$ exactly when $I\subseteq\ker f$. In particular $R/\ker f\cong f[R]$ by $r+\ker f\mapsto f(r)$. The quotient is commutative if $R$ is commutative.

nodes.label: Correspondence and iterated quotients of rings
nodes.statement: For a two-sided ideal $I$, ideals of $R/I$ correspond by inverse image to ideals of $R$ containing $I$, with left, right and two-sided versions. Subrings of $R/I$ correspond to subrings containing $I$. If $I\subseteq J$ are two-sided ideals, then $(R/I)/(J/I)\cong R/J$. If $S$ is a subring and $I$ a two-sided ideal of $R$, then $S/(S\cap I)\cong(S+I)/I$.

nodes.label: Integral domain / Anneau intègre
nodes.statement: An integral domain is a commutative ring with $0\ne1$ in which $ab=0$ implies $a=0$ or $b=0$. Thus it has no nonzero zero divisors. The integers form an integral domain.

nodes.label: Division ring / Corps, éventuellement non commutatif
nodes.statement: A division ring is a nonzero ring in which every nonzero element is invertible. This is the notion called **field** in Bourbaki I, §9, no. 1. Its multiplication is not assumed commutative. Its nonzero elements form a group, and its additive group remains abelian.

nodes.label: Commutative field / Corps commutatif
nodes.statement: A commutative field is a division ring whose multiplication is commutative. It is simultaneously an integral domain and a division ring. In the usual two-operation language, its additive structure is an abelian group and its nonzero multiplicative structure is an abelian group, with distributivity joining the operations.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §9, no. 1, with commutativity explicitly added.

bibliography.locator: I, §9, no. 1, with commutativity explicitly added.

direct_dependencies.note: Immediate parent structure explicitly used in this definition.
uses [AS-A02](#as-a02)

nodes.label: Subfield, generated subfield and field embedding
nodes.statement: A subfield of a commutative field $K$ is a subring closed under inverses of nonzero elements. Its own operations are those induced from $K$. The subfield generated by $X\subseteq K$ is the intersection of subfields containing $X$. A field homomorphism is a ring homomorphism between fields; it is automatically injective and is called an embedding. The same substructure definition, without commutativity, gives a division subring of a division ring.

nodes.label: Field of fractions / Corps des fractions
nodes.statement:
For a domain $A$, define $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ from pairs $(a,b)$ with $b\ne0$, identifying $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ when $ad=bc$. Write $a/b$ for a class. Put
$$\frac ab+\frac cd=\frac{ad+bc}{bd},\qquad \frac ab\frac cd=\frac{ac}{bd},\qquad -\frac ab=\frac{-a}{b}.$$
For $a\ne0$ the inverse of $a/b$ is $b/a$. The map $a\mapsto a/1$ is the canonical embedding. The nonzero denominators need no positivity convention, since a general domain has no specified order.

nodes.label: Maximal ideal / Idéal maximal
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring $R$, an ideal $\mathfrak m$ is maximal if $\mathfrak m\ne R$ and no ideal lies strictly between $\mathfrak m$ and $R$. Properness is part of the definition. The zero ring has no maximal ideals.

nodes.label: Prime ideal / Idéal premier
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring $R$, an ideal $\mathfrak p$ is prime if $\mathfrak p\ne R$ and $ab\in\mathfrak p$ implies $a\in\mathfrak p$ or $b\in\mathfrak p$. This is the commutative definition; no noncommutative prime-ideal theory is developed here.

nodes.label: Characteristic / Caractéristique
nodes.statement: The characteristic of a ring $R$ is the least positive integer $n$ with $n1_R=0_R$, if one exists; otherwise it is $0$. Here $n1_R$ denotes repeated addition. Equivalently, the kernel of $\mathbb Z\to R$, $n\mapsto n1_R$, is $\operatorname{char}(R)\mathbb Z$. The zero ring has characteristic $1$.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §8, no. 4, for the canonical map from $\mathbb Z$; §9 for its use in fields. The definition here records the kernel invariant explicitly.

bibliography.locator: I, §8, no. 4, for the canonical map from $\mathbb Z$; §9 for its use in fields. The definition here records the kernel invariant explicitly.

nodes.label: Prime subfield / Sous-corps premier
nodes.statement: The prime subfield of a commutative field $K$ is its smallest subfield, the subfield generated by $1$. It is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$ in characteristic zero and to $\mathbb F_p=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ in characteristic $p>0$. A prime integer means an integer $p>1$ whose positive divisors are $1$ and $p$.
nodes.reference: [B](#bib-b), I, §9, nos. 1 and 4, for the prime finite fields and the rational field; the prime-subfield statement combines these constructions.

nodes.label: Cancellation in domains and division rings
nodes.statement: In a domain, every nonzero element is cancellable under multiplication. A division ring has no nonzero zero divisors; hence a commutative field is a domain. A finite integral domain is a field: multiplication by a nonzero element is injective on the finite set and therefore takes some element to $1$. This last result does not assert that every finite division ring is commutative; that stronger theorem is deferred.

nodes.label: Division rings, ideals and injectivity of field maps
nodes.statement: A nonzero ring is a division ring exactly when its only left ideals are $\{0\}$ and itself; the analogous right-ideal statement also holds. In particular, a unital homomorphism from a division ring to a nonzero ring is injective. Intersections of subfields inside a fixed field are subfields, so generated subfields exist. For a commutative ring, being a field is equivalent to being nonzero and having no nonzero proper ideal.

nodes.label: Existence and universal property of the fraction field
nodes.statement: The fraction relation and operations in `AS-D39` are well-defined, make $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ a commutative field, and embed $A$ injectively. Every embedding $f\colon A\to K$ into a commutative field extends uniquely to a field embedding $\widetilde f\colon\operatorname{Frac}(A)\to K$ by $a/b\mapsto f(a)f(b)^{-1}$. Its image is the subfield generated by $f[A]$. In particular $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Q$, compatibly with the NS construction using positive denominators.

nodes.label: Prime and maximal ideals through quotients
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring $R$ and an ideal $I$, the quotient $R/I$ is a domain exactly when $I$ is prime, and it is a field exactly when $I$ is maximal. Therefore every maximal ideal is prime. In $\mathbb Z$, $(0)$ is prime but is not maximal. For $n\ge2$, $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is a field exactly when $n$ is prime.

nodes.label: The integer map, characteristic and prime subfields
nodes.statement: Every ring $R$ admits exactly one unital ring homomorphism $\mathbb Z\to R$, given by $n\mapsto n1_R$. Its kernel has the form $n\mathbb Z$, identifying $n=\operatorname{char}(R)$. If $R$ is a domain or a division ring, this characteristic is zero or a prime integer. For a commutative field of characteristic $p$, the image is its prime subfield $\mathbb F_p$. In characteristic zero, the integer embedding extends uniquely to an embedding of $\mathbb Q$, whose image is the prime subfield. Thus the characteristics of $\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ are zero.

nodes.label: Existence of maximal ideals / Théorème de Krull
nodes.statement: **Background: ZFC; the proof recorded here uses Zorn's lemma.** Every proper ideal $I$ of a nonzero commutative ring $R$ is contained in a maximal ideal. Order the proper ideals containing $I$ by inclusion; the union of any nonempty chain is an ideal and remains proper because it does not contain $1$. Zorn's lemma then applies. In particular every nonzero commutative ring has a quotient that is a field. This use of choice is a sufficient proof background, with no claim that full choice is the weakest possible assumption.

nodes.label: Group completion of a cancellative commutative monoid
nodes.statement:
Write a cancellative commutative monoid $M$ additively, with identity $0$. On $M\times M$ put $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ when $a+d=c+b$. Define $G(M)=(M\times M)/{\sim}$, with
$$[a,b]+[c,d]=[a+c,b+d],\qquad -[a,b]=[b,a].$$
The natural map is $j(a)=[a,0]$. This is the cancellative case of Bourbaki's monoid of differences, obtained by making all elements invertible. For a noncancellative commutative monoid the equivalence relation needs an extra common summand; that generalisation is deferred.

nodes.label: Group-completion theorem and the integers
nodes.statement: The construction $G(M)$ is an abelian group, and $j$ is an injective monoid homomorphism. For every monoid homomorphism $f\colon M\to H$ into an abelian group, there is a unique group homomorphism $\bar f\colon G(M)\to H$ satisfying $\bar f\circ j=f$, namely $\bar f([a,b])=f(a)-f(b)$. For $(\mathbb N,+,0)$ this is the additive integer group constructed in NS. Multiplication on $\mathbb Z$ is additional data, supplied there by its separate formula.

nodes.label: Algebraic structures carried by the number systems
nodes.statement: With the operations constructed in NS, $(\mathbb N,+,0)$ is a cancellative commutative monoid, and $(\mathbb N,\cdot,1)$ is a commutative monoid whose cancellable elements are the positive naturals. The additive integers are an abelian group; their two operations make $\mathbb Z$ a domain. The systems $\mathbb Q,\mathbb R,\mathbb C$ are commutative fields. The maps $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ are injective unital ring homomorphisms; between fields they are field embeddings. The map $\mathbb N\to\mathbb Z$ preserves each monoid operation. No ring structure on $\mathbb N$ with its usual operations is asserted, because additive inverses are missing.

nodes.label: Forgetting structure and the boundary with order
nodes.statement: Forgetting inverses turns a group into a monoid; forgetting the identity turns a monoid into an associative magma; forgetting associativity leaves a magma. A ring has an additive abelian group and a multiplicative monoid on the same set. For a field, its multiplicative group is on the nonzero elements only. The order axioms of NS are additional structure: the field axioms do not prescribe an order, and the usual complex field admits no total order compatible with its arithmetic.
